title: Operator Precedence and Complex Conditions
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of operator precedence and complex conditions.
Apply arithmetic precedence in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn operator precedence and complex conditions through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Operator Precedence and Complex Conditions matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The practical goal of operator precedence and complex conditions is to produce a result set whose meaning is clear. Confirm which rows enter the query, how values are transformed or combined, and whether NULLs, duplicates, ties, or one-to-many relationships change the output.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Arithmetic precedence, Comparison and logical precedence, Parentheses for clarity, Common Boolean logic bugs. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Arithmetic precedence
items.text: Arithmetic precedence helps you express precise conditions with comparison, logical, range, membership, pattern, NULL-safe, and CASE expressions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Common Boolean logic bugs
items.text: Common Boolean logic bugs works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Testing complex conditions
items.text: Testing complex conditions makes SQL easier to change safely. Turn assumptions into repeatable checks, keep schema/query changes reviewable, use deterministic ordering, and record the data shape and environment used for the check.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT product_id, name, price
FROM products
WHERE price >= 25 AND is_active = TRUE
ORDER BY price DESC, product_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query filters active products at or above the chosen price threshold, then sorts the remaining rows.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic arithmetic precedence and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
